title: Compound Interest Calculator
story: You just opened a savings account and the banker mentions 'compound interest.' Instead of trusting their math, you build your own calculator that shows exactly how your money grows year by year — using a while loop inside a function.
why: Functions with loops inside them demonstrate how algorithms can be encapsulated — the caller only cares about the result, not how many iterations it took.
analogy: Compound interest is like a snowball rolling downhill. Each rotation (year) picks up more snow (interest), and the bigger snowball picks up even more snow next rotation. The function is the hill — you tell it the starting size, slope, and number of rotations; it tells you the final snowball.
try_it: Modify `calc_interest` to also return how much total interest was earned (final balance minus principal). Test with a 1000.0 principal at 10% for 20 years.
tips: Use Float64 for financial calculations — rounding errors with Int would be catastrophic
The loop counter `y` must start at 0 and increment each iteration — otherwise infinite loop
Hide complexity: the caller passes 3 numbers and gets 1 result — everything else is internal
The growth factor is `1.0 + rate`: a 5% rate means multiply by 1.05
common_mistakes: Forgetting to use `1.0 + rate` — multiplying by just `rate` would SHRINK the balance
Using Int for balance — you'll lose all cents and compound growth
Not incrementing the year counter `y` inside the loop — infinite loop
Confusing the rate format: 0.05 means 5%, not 5.0 (which would be 500%)
